intuition: First remember each node's parent. Mark the ancestors of the first target, including the target itself. Then walk upward from the second target. The first marked node you reach is their lowest shared ancestor, because you encounter nearer ancestors before higher ones.

An iterative traversal records each discovered node’s parent by identity. Once p and q are discovered, those records already include their complete chains to the root. Mark every ancestor of p, including p itself, then walk upward from q.

The first marked node encountered from q is the lowest common ancestor: any later shared node is strictly higher on q’s chain. Using original node objects rather than values preserves the required identity. A target that is itself above the other target naturally becomes the answer because nodes count as their own ancestors.

steps: Use root=[10,5,3,8,2], p=node 8, and q=node 2. Initialize parents[root]=None and stack=[10].
Pop 10 and record parents[5]=10 and parents[3]=10. The stack contains 5 then 3.
Pop 3, which has no children. Pop 5 next and record parents[8]=5 and parents[2]=5.
Both targets are now discovered, so stop building parents. Walk from p=8 upward and mark nodes 8,5,10.
Start the second walk at q=2. It is not marked, so follow its parent to node 5.
Node 5 is marked and is the first shared node encountered. Return the original node 5, displayed by its value in the fixture.

concept.correctness: The marked set is exactly the first target’s ancestors, including itself. Climbing from the second visits its ancestors in increasing distance.
